    AI Overview
    +5
    The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) of 1978 is a U.S. federal law establishing procedures for physical and electronic surveillance of foreign intelligence information. It allows government agencies, like the NSA and FBI, to conduct surveillance on foreign powers and agents without traditional warrants, often targeting communications outside the U.S. that may include Americans. 
    Key Aspects of FISA: 
    • Purpose: Created to regulate surveillance aimed at collecting foreign intelligence, rather than criminal evidence.
    • FISA Court (FISC): Specialized federal court that reviews government applications for surveillance orders
      .
    • Section 702 (Controversial): A key, often-renewed provision that allows the government to compel U.S. companies to provide data on non-U.S. persons located outside the U.S..
    • Incidental Surveillance: In the process of targeting foreigners, the government often collects information on U.S. citizens.
    • Oversight: While overseen by all three branches, it is a subject of intense debate over privacy, with critics calling it mass surveillance of Americans. 
    FISA was enacted after intelligence abuses were revealed in the 1970s and has been significantly amended over time.

    AI Overview
    The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) of 1978 establishes legal procedures and oversight for federal government agencies to conduct physical searches and electronic surveillance of foreign powers and their agents within the U.S.. It aims to balance national security with civil liberties, often requiring warrants from the secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC). 
    Key functions of FISA include: 
    • Surveillance Authority: Authorizes surveillance of foreign agents or powers, including wiretapping and tracking digital communication.
    • FISA Court (FISC): Operates a specialized court of 11 federal district judges who review and approve government applications for surveillance warrants
      .
    • Section 702 Authority: Enables intelligence agencies (like the NSA and FBI) to target non-U.S. persons located outside the U.S. to acquire foreign intelligence information, often without an individualized warrant.
    • Oversight and Minimization: Requires procedures to minimize the acquisition, retention, and dissemination of nonpublic information about U.S. citizens who may be incidentally caught in surveillance. 
    FISA is frequently used to investigate terrorism and espionage. However, Section 702 is controversial, with critics raising concerns about the potential for "backdoor" searches of American communications without a warrant.
